conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 gentle questions about your mood, thoughts, and well-being over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything stays confidential between you and our team, and we can pause any time you need. Ready to start?

First, I’d love to know: over the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

Hi, Sarah. I… I can still laugh sometimes, but it feels like it takes more effort than it used to. Like, if my husband makes a joke while we’re folding the baby’s laundry, I’ll smile or even chuckle, but it doesn’t come as easily. It feels kind of forced, like I’m reminding myself it’s okay to laugh. So I guess I can still see the funny side, but it’s definitely not as natural or spontaneous as before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most of the time I can still laugh, but it doesn’t feel quite the same—like I have to think about it first.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like when my mom comes over to hold the baby so I can take a shower—but it’s not that excited, happy feeling I used to get. It’s more like, “Okay, that’ll be nice,” rather than really looking forward to it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking maybe I’m doing something wrong—like if I were a better mom he’d sleep. I know it’s probably not true, but the thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Sometimes I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my chest feels tight, thinking “What if she spits up and chokes when I’m not looking?” Nothing’s happening, but my mind races anyway.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of nights I’ve woken up suddenly with my heart racing, sure something was wrong with the baby—even though she was right there in the bassinet, breathing fine. It only lasts a minute or two, but it feels scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… some days it feels like the dirty bottles, laundry, and night-wakings just pile up faster than I can handle them. I’m not falling apart, but I do catch myself thinking, “How am I going to keep doing this?” a few times a week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “so unhappy,” but I do lie there once the baby’s finally down and my mind keeps ticking through all the what-ifs—what if he wakes early, what if I miss something, what if I’m doing this all wrong. It takes me a while to drift off, and then I wake up at every tiny grunt over the monitor.
I have felt sad or miserable

I get little waves of sadness—like when I’m rocking her at 3 a.m. and suddenly feel like I’m failing even though she’s peacefully asleep. It’s not all day, but those moments hit me a few times since last week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t actually cried. I’ve felt teary a couple of times—like my throat gets tight and my eyes sting—but the tears never quite come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that, over the past week, moments of joy feel dulled-laughter requires effort, anticipated pleasures no longer spark excitement, and brief "waves of sadness" or worry pop up unexpectedly. You described blaming yourself when your baby wouldn't settle, feeling your chest tighten with anxious "what-ifs" during feeds, waking in a rush of panic, and lying awake ruminating. Despite these struggles, you continue to care lovingly for your infant and have not had thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She still anticipates events but reports the loss of the prior "excited, happy feeling," matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurrent self-blame "a few times" in the past week, specifically linking baby's nap struggles to personal inadequacy, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, intrusive worries without real danger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes discrete nocturnal panic episodes occurring multiple times, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, concrete stressors (bottles, laundry, night-wakings) piling up faster than she can manage and recurrent thoughts of "How am I going to keep doing this?"—semantic match for "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep driven by persistent anxious thoughts, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 places you above the 13-point cutoff that flags probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse five core depressive symptoms (<sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>loss of enjoyment</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>insomnia</sym>, <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>) plus prominent anxiety, meeting partial <med>DSM-5</med> criteria. Because symptoms cluster several days per week and impair sleep and confidence, urgent evaluation is recommended. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to discuss mood and anxiety since delivery
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full diagnostic assessment and treatment planning
3. Continue regular check-ins with your support team (partner, family, midwife) and share how you're feeling
4. Practice small, achievable self-care: 5-minute outdoor walk, balanced snacks, accepting help with chores
5. Consider peer support groups (local mothers' circle or online postpartum communities)
6. Schedule EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks to track any changes
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report, 2–3 wks post-delivery

Symptoms endorsed  
• Anhedonia / diminished enjoyment (Q2)  
• Subjective low mood, “waves of sadness,” tearfulness without overt crying (Q8, Q9)  
• Excessive self-blame / guilt (Q3)  
• Generalized & infant-focused anxiety, nocturnal panic (Q4, Q5)  
• Sleep-onset & maintenance difficulties tied to ruminating worries (Q7)  
• Feeling overwhelmed, doubts about coping (Q6)  
• No anhedonia in every situation—still able to laugh, though effortful (Q1)  
• No current suicidal or self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate mood distress with prominent anxiety; symptoms present several days per week, interfere with sleep and sense of competence, but not incapacitating.

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for postpartum depression (sad mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep disturbance) and postpartum anxiety; intensity below threshold for severe episode but sufficient to warrant further assessment.

Safety  
Denies self-harm; no acute safety concerns identified.

Recommendation  
Continue monitoring; consider full diagnostic interview (DSM-5-TR) for major depressive disorder with peripartum onset and/or anxiety disorder; provide psycho-education and support resources; re-screen in 2 weeks or sooner if worsening.
